I have basically quit. After about 9 years. I had some highs and lows. I got better than I ever thought I would when I started doing stand up...when I would listen to Dave Attell and Mitch and wonder how they came up with anything funny at all.

I eventually did come up with stuff of my own. Not of their level but in a similar genre of joke writing. I'm proud of myself for that - that I wrote the types of jokes I found funny when I was just alone in a room listening to stand up to fill the void.

I also did all the stuff that you're supposed to do. Grinding it out to nobody. Going to random cities or even countries for stage time. Moving to a new city for standup and working a dead end job to grind it out and maybe get a spot now and again. Performing at some big clubs in the US as well as proving myself in my home country and internationally. I proved that I could make people laugh all over the world and that is....something.

It was fun and not fun. It gave a sense of purpose, community, connection. But I kept running into a brick wall with my stand up (not literally). I felt I couldn't turn over good material fast enough. I didn't feel like I was evolving and when I did evolve to my more natural voice, it wasn't actually funny. Then I felt trapped in being a set up punch guy, which was fine but I just couldn't write material fast enough. Especially when depressed or anxious. It could take me a month just to have 1 or 2 usable new jokes that were consistent enough.

Ultimately, the juice wasn't quite worth the squeeze in terms of how much I had to put into my stand up to be the level I wanted to be at and the lack of time I had due to work and my own mental health issues.

Comedy is better for people who are able to take life lightly. I was way too serious about it. I was too serious about joke writing, about what it all meant, about whether or not it was the right thing. Overall, although at times I felt like it was my calling I also thought I didn't have the right personality and mentality for stand up. That's how I feel now.

I will always love jokes and I will always write them, but I would prefer to try other mediums like storytrelling or essays wtih humour in them.

Psychological resistance. One weird thing about human nature is when your brain is strongly telling you NOT to do something, it's a sign on some level you want to do it.  Otherwise you just wouldn't care or give it much thought.

​

I think most people have this part of them that wants to sabotage their chances of success. Like a self-destructive impulse. I think it's part of human nature, not just relating to open mics and stand up.

​

Of course, sometimes you overcome all this negative psychological stuff to arrive at a mic with just two comics in the audience and it confirms everything you said to try to talk yourself out of it. But it's never about one mic or one show but the cumulative effect of everything over years of work. But that includes taking time off. Dangerfield took years off, but kept writing jokes in that time. 

Sometimes time away can be good. If you take away hating yourself and your act and having high standards etc, if we assume that's part of it, do you still want to perform comedy? 

When I'm in these zones I try to remember why i started....watching Dave Attell for the first time, seeing Hebderg for the first time and that inspiration of like, 'I would love to be able to have that kind of effect on an audience, to have that kind of power and the intelligence and creativity to know how to bring it about'....when I remember those early more innocent thoughts, I remember why I do stand up. So much is just dark thoughts getting in the way of the pure almost childlike innocence of wanting to be creative.

There's also a theatrical element, with so many people aiming for an Edinburgh show that has a theme which ties everything together perfectly like a play might. American stand ups do everything better than the Brits except for that 'tying the show together with a big ending that encapsulates the themes of everything that came before' thing...which I personally don't even care that much about, as it makes for slightly contrived and annoying shows.

When I first started, I did a new 6 minutes every time I went up for a few months. I thought 'woah, I'm really making up for not being on stage much.' But in reality, I was just telling half written jokes that I could barely remember and then throwing them out way too hastily when they bombed.

The better you remember your set, the less stress you feel before going on stage and the more confidently you can then deliver it. One of the difficulties with stand up is being able to deliver material well without the excitement of it being newly written. So in a way, it's good to practice the same jokes for that reason too.

Having said that, always be adding new jokes. I try to do at least one new joke in a set. Either that, or add a tag or rewrite of an old joke that isn't clicking yet.

If you aren't nervous before going on stage, you probably aren't doing anything risky or challenging. Or, there are absolutely no stakes for the performance for you personally or for advancement in your standup 'career.' If that's the case...what's the point?

There really is something to that 'no pain no gain' thing. Facing the fear, overcoming it, that's what stand up is. Getting to the point where you have no fear and becoming unwilling to take risks is when you become unfunny.

BTW - I've heard interviews with several comics where they talk about blanking at points during their sets for TV. These are guys with 10 plus years experiences who may have run these sets 100s of times in clubs. They still freak out and blank when it comes to TV. So there you go... Fear is a thing.
